scripts.topic: Why Plastic Rulers Smear Gel Ink (And the Capillary Gap Fix)
scripts.text: Dragging your ruler across fresh ink is not what ruins your exam diagrams. Gel pens deposit liquid ink that sits on the paper surface, and pressing down flat plastic traps it instantly. Friction does not cause the smear. Capillary action pulls the wet ink into the microscopic gap between flat plastic and paper fibers. You can easily defeat this surface tension. Stick two layers of transparent tape 1 mm behind the beveled measurement edge on the ruler's underside to create a 0.3 mm air gap that breaks the ink meniscus. Blowing on the page will not protect your graphs. Flip your ruler over right now and apply those tape strips.

scripts.topic: Why Peeling Sticky Notes Sideways Stops Them Falling Off Study Walls
scripts.text: Your sticky notes keep falling off study walls because of how you peel them. Most students grab the bottom corner and yank upward, only to find their formula sheets on the floor hours later. When you pull vertically, you bend the paper fibers past their elastic limit. That permanent curl creates spring tension that constantly fights the weak pressure-sensitive glue. Instead, pull horizontally from left to right along the 76 mm adhesive strip instead of pulling vertically from the bottom edge. Smoothing it down harder will not fix it once the paper fibers are bent. Peel your next reminder sideways right now and stick it flat against your monitor.
